standing_assumptions: Setting. The work is a textbook: Aronow and Miller, Foundations of Agnostic Statistics (Cambridge University Press, 2019). Every statement is about random variables on a probability space; Part II adds i.i.d. sampling; Part III adds the missing-data and potential-outcomes models. Locations give the printed page and the one-based page of main.pdf (316 pp.; in the body, PDF page = printed page + 18). Statements were transcribed from the page images (the 110 dpi staged renders, with higher-resolution renders of the same PDF pages where subscripts were small) and compared with the text layer for wording. (S1) Probability space. [Definition 1.1.1, p. 6 (PDF p. 24)] A set $S$ of subsets of $\Omega$ is an event space if it satisfies the following: Nonempty: $S \ne \emptyset$. Closed under complements: if $A \in S$, then $A^C \in S$. Closed under countable unions: if $A_1, A_2, A_3, ... \in S$, then $A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup ... \in S$. [Definition 1.1.2, p. 7 (PDF p. 25)] Kolmogorov Axioms. Let $\Omega$ be a sample space, $S$ be an event space, and $P$ be a probability measure. Then $(\Omega, S, P)$ is a probability space if it satisfies the following: Non-negativity: $\forall A \in S$, $P(A) \ge 0$, where $P(A)$ is finite and real. Unitarity: $P(\Omega) = 1$. Countable additivity: if $A_1, A_2, A_3, ... \in S$ are pairwise disjoint, then $P(A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup ...) = P(A_1) + P(A_2) + P(A_3) + ... = \sum_i P(A_i)$. [Footnote 11, p. 8 (PDF p. 26)] This assumption [that $(\Omega, S, P)$ is a probability space] shall henceforth be implicit in all definitions and theorems referring to $\Omega$, $S$, and/or $P$. (S2) Random variables and their distributions. [Definition 1.2.1, p. 16 (PDF p. 34)] A random variable is a function $X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ such that, $\forall r \in \mathbb{R}$, $\{\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) \le r\} \in S$. [Definition 1.2.2, p. 16] Let $g : U \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function, where $X(\Omega) \subseteq U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. Then, if $g \circ X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ is a random variable, we say that $g$ is a function of $X$, and write $g(X)$ to denote the random variable $g \circ X$. [p. 17 (PDF p. 35)] we use $\Pr[\cdot]$ to denote the probability that some condition(s) on a random variable will hold, or, equivalently, the probability that the event defined by those conditions will occur. [Definition 1.2.4, p. 18 (PDF p. 36)] A random variable $X$ is discrete if its range, $X(\Omega)$, is a countable set. [Definition 1.2.5, p. 18] For a discrete random variable $X$, the probability mass function of $X$ is $f(x) = \Pr[X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.11, p. 21 (PDF p. 39)] For a random variable $X$, the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is $F(x) = \Pr[X \le x]$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.14, p. 24 (PDF p. 42)] A random variable $X$ is continuous if there exists a non-negative function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that the CDF of $X$ is $F(x) = \Pr[X \le x] = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f(u)du$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. The function $f$ is called the probability density function (PDF). [Definition 1.2.15, p. 25 (PDF p. 43), as printed; see finding P001-C01-E002] For a continuous random variable $X$ with CDF $F$, the probability density function of $X$ is $f(x) = \left.\frac{dF(u)}{du}\right|_{u=x}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.20, p. 31 (PDF p. 49)] For a random variable $X$ with PMF/PDF $f$, the support of $X$ is $\mathrm{Supp}[X] = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : f(x) > 0\}$. [Definition 1.3.1, p. 31] Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. Then $X = Y$ if, $\forall\omega \in \Omega$, $X(\omega) = Y(\omega)$. [Definition 1.3.16, p. 38 (PDF p. 56)] Let $X$ and $Y$ be either two discrete random variables with joint PMF $f$ or two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF $f$. Then $X$ and $Y$ are independent if, $\forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}$, $f(x, y) = f_X(x)f_Y(y)$. We write $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y$. [Definition 1.4.1, p. 39 (PDF p. 57)] A random vector (of length $K$) is a function $\mathbf{X} : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^K$ such that, $\forall\omega \in \Omega$, $\mathbf{X}(\omega) = (X_{[1]}(\omega), X_{[2]}(\omega), ..., X_{[K]}(\omega))$, where $\forall k \in \{1, 2, ..., K\}$, $X_{[k]}$ is a random variable. (S3) Expectations. [Definition 2.1.1, p. 45 (PDF p. 63)] For a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function (PMF) $f$, if $\sum_x |x|f(x) < \infty$, then the expected value of $X$ is $\mathrm{E}[X] = \sum_x xf(x)$. For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function (PDF) $f$, if $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |x|f(x)dx < \infty$, then the expected value of $X$ is $\mathrm{E}[X] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} xf(x)dx$. [Footnote 2, p. 45] This regularity condition (and the corresponding one in the continuous case) is known as absolute convergence. It is virtually always satisfied in practice, so we omit this technical condition from all subsequent discussion of expectations. [Footnote 3, p. 49 (PDF p. 67)] This theorem, and every subsequent theorem that we only prove for these two cases [two discrete random variables with joint PMF, or two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF], also holds when one random variable is discrete and the other continuous. [Definition 2.1.12, p. 52 (PDF p. 70)] The variance of a random variable $X$ is $\mathrm{V}[X] = \mathrm{E}[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])^2]$. [Definition 2.1.15, p. 53 (PDF p. 71)] The standard deviation of a random variable $X$ is $\sigma[X] = \sqrt{\mathrm{V}[X]}$. [Definition 2.1.22, p. 57 (PDF p. 75)] For a random variable $X$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$, the mean squared error of $X$ about $c$ is $\mathrm{E}[(X - c)^2]$. [Definition 2.2.1, p. 59 (PDF p. 77)] The covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is $\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y] = \mathrm{E}[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y])]$. [Definition 2.2.5, p. 62 (PDF p. 80)] The correlation of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ with $\sigma[X] > 0$ and $\sigma[Y] > 0$ is $\rho[X, Y] = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y]}{\sigma[X]\sigma[Y]}$. [Definition 2.2.10, p. 67 (PDF p. 85)] For discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF $f$, the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = \sum_y yf_{Y|X}(y|x)$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. For jointly continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PDF $f$, the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} yf_{Y|X}(y|x)dy$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 2.2.12, p. 68 (PDF p. 86)] For random variables $X$ and $Y$, the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{V}[Y|X = x] = \mathrm{E}[(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x])^2|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 2.2.15, p. 69 (PDF p. 87)] For random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF/PDF $f$, the conditional expectation function of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $G_Y(x) = \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [p. 70 (PDF p. 88)] We write $\mathrm{E}[Y|X]$ to denote $G_Y(X)$; the conditional variance function is $H_Y(x) = \mathrm{V}[Y|X = x]$, and $\mathrm{V}[Y|X]$ denotes the random variable $H_Y(X)$. [Footnote 14, p. 70] Ignoring some unimportant measure-theoretic regularity conditions, namely $X(\Omega) = \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. The multivariate versions are Definitions 2.3.3 and 2.3.4 (p. 85, PDF p. 103) and the multivariate BLP, Definition 2.3.6 (p. 86, PDF p. 104; transcribed in the targets that use it). (S4) Sampling and asymptotics. [Definition 3.1.1, p. 92 (PDF p. 110)] Let $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ be random variables with CDFs $F_1, F_2, ..., F_n$, respectively. Let $F_A$ denote the joint CDF of the random variables with indices in the set $A$. Then $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ are independent and identically distributed if they satisfy the following: Mutually independent: $\forall A \subseteq \{1, 2, ..., n\}$, $\forall(x_1, x_2, ..., x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $F_A((x_i)_{i \in A}) = \prod_{i \in A} F_i(x_i)$. Identically distributed: $\forall i, j \in \{1, 2, ..., n\}$ and $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$, $F_i(x) = F_j(x)$. [p. 92] When we have i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, we use the unsubscripted letter $X$ to denote the random variable whose distribution the i.i.d. draws all share. So, for example, $\mathrm{E}[X]$ denotes the expected value common to $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, that is, $\mathrm{E}[X] = \mathrm{E}[X_1] = \mathrm{E}[X_2] = ... = \mathrm{E}[X_n]$. [Definition 3.2.1, p. 96 (PDF p. 114)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, a sample statistic is a function of $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$: $T_{(n)} = h_{(n)}(X_1, X_2, ..., X_n)$, where $h_{(n)} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$, $\forall n \in \mathbb{N}$. [Definition 3.2.2, p. 97 (PDF p. 115)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, the sample mean is $\overline{X} = \frac{X_1 + X_2 + ... + X_n}{n} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i$. [Definition 3.2.6, p. 99 (PDF p. 117)] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables and let $c \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in probability to $c$ if, $\forall\epsilon > 0$, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[|T_{(n)} - c| \ge \epsilon] = 0$, or equivalently, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[|T_{(n)} - c| < \epsilon] = 1$; written $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{p} c$. [Definition 3.2.22, p. 108 (PDF p. 126)] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables with CDFs $(F_{(1)}, F_{(2)}, F_{(3)}, ...)$, and let $T$ be a random variable with CDF $F$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in distribution to $T$ if, $\forall t \in \mathbb{R}$ at which $F$ is continuous, $\lim_{n \to \infty} F_{(n)}(t) = F(t)$; written $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{d} T$. [Definition 3.2.28, p. 112 (PDF p. 130)] An estimator $\hat\theta$ is asymptotically normal if $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \phi^2)$, for some finite $\phi > 0$. [Definition 3.3.1, p. 116 (PDF p. 134)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, the empirical CDF $\hat F$ of $X$ is $\hat F(x) = \overline{\mathrm{I}(X \le x)}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 3.3.2, p. 118 (PDF p. 136)] A statistical functional is a function $T : \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathcal{F}$ is the set of all possible CDFs. [Definition 3.3.3, p. 118] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ with common CDF $F$, the plug-in estimator of $\theta = T(F)$ is $\hat\theta = T(\hat F)$. The 'usual plug-in regularity conditions' (p. 120, PDF p. 138) are not formally defined in the book (footnote 31 names Hadamard differentiability with respect to the Kolmogorov distance and gives no formal definition). (S5) Regression. [Definition 4.1.2, pp. 146–147 (PDF pp. 164–165), with the plus sign before the last term supplied] For i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), (Y_2, \mathbf{X}_2), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$, the ordinary least squares (OLS) regression estimator is the function $\hat g(\mathbf{X}) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1X_{[1]} + \hat\beta_2X_{[2]} + ... + \hat\beta_KX_{[K]}$ such that $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1, ..., \hat\beta_K) = \arg\min_{(b_0, b_1, ..., b_K) \in \mathbb{R}^{K+1}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_i - (b_0 + b_1X_{[1]i} + b_2X_{[2]i} + ... + b_KX_{[K]i})\right)^2$. We refer to $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ as the OLS coefficient estimator. [Definition 4.1.3, p. 148 (PDF p. 166)] the regressor matrix $\mathbb{X}$ is the $n \times (K + 1)$ matrix whose $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ row is $(1, X_{[1]i}, X_{[2]i}, \cdots, X_{[K]i})$. (S6) Parametric models. [Definition 5.1.1, pp. 178–179 (PDF pp. 196–197)] For a random variable $Y$ and random vector $\mathbf{X}$ of length $K$, a parametric model is a set of functions $g : \mathbb{R}^{K+1} \to \mathbb{R}$ indexed by a real-valued parameter vector $\boldsymbol\theta$ of length $\tau$: $\{g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta) : \boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta\}$, where $\boldsymbol\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^\tau$. The set $\boldsymbol\Theta$ is called the parameter space. The model is said to be true if $\exists\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$ such that $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$. [Definition 5.2.1, p. 186 (PDF p. 204)] the likelihood function is $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y, \mathbf{X}) = g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})$, and for i.i.d. observations $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. [Definition 5.2.2, pp. 186–187 (PDF pp. 204–205)] the maximum likelihood estimator of $\boldsymbol\theta$ is $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. (S7) Missing data. [Definition 6.1.1, pp. 208–209 (PDF pp. 226–227)] For an outcome variable $Y_i$, the stable outcomes model is $Y_i^* = -99$ if $R_i = 0$ and $Y_i$ if $R_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$, where $Y_i^*$ is the censored version of $Y_i$ and $R_i$ is an indicator for whether $Y_i$ is observed for unit $i$. [Footnote 2, p. 208] Since we are assuming i.i.d. sampling, our inferences do not depend on the unit subscript $i$. [Definition 6.1.5, p. 213 (PDF p. 231)] $Y_i$ is missing completely at random if $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i$ and $\Pr[R_i = 1] > 0$. [Definition 6.1.8, p. 215 (PDF p. 233)] $Y_i$ is missing at random conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] > \epsilon$. [Footnote 6, p. 215] For random variables $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ with joint PMF/PDF $f(x, y, z)$, $Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z|X$ if, $\forall y, z \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$, $f_{(Y,Z)|X}((y, z)|x) = f_{Y|X}(y|x)f_{Z|X}(z|x)$. [Definition 6.1.11, p. 217 (PDF p. 235)] the response propensity function is $p_R(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. (S8) Causal inference. [Definition 7.1.1, p. 236 (PDF p. 254)] For an outcome variable $Y_i$ and binary treatment variable $D_i$, the potential outcomes model is $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$, where $Y_i(0)$ denotes the potential outcome under control for unit $i$, and $Y_i(1)$ denotes the potential outcome under treatment for unit $i$. [Definition 7.1.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 255)] $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. [Definition 7.1.3, p. 238 (PDF p. 256)] the average treatment effect (ATE) is $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$. [Definition 7.1.9, p. 244 (PDF p. 262)] $D_i$ is randomly assigned if $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i$ and $0 < \Pr[D_i = 1] < 1$. [Definition 7.1.12, p. 247 (PDF p. 265)] $D_i$ is strongly ignorable conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\epsilon < \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] < 1 - \epsilon$. [Definition 7.1.15, p. 250 (PDF p. 268)] the treatment propensity function is $p_D(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. Notes for the formalizer. (a) The book works with PMFs and PDFs and states pointwise conditions ('for all $x$'); for continuous variables these hold only up to null sets (finding P001-C01-E002), so a measure-theoretic formalization should read densities and conditional expectations as versions. (b) Existence and finiteness of the expectations in a statement is a standing convention (footnote 2, p. 45). (c) Asymptotic statements are about an infinite i.i.d. sequence and $n \to \infty$. (d) In a target's statement, text in square brackets is a label or a remark of the transcriber, not the book's words.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Definition 3.3.9 (Kernel Plug-In Estimator) with the kernels admitted by Definition 3.3.7, as printed: a signed kernel for which $\hat F_K$ is not a CDF
canonical_claim.location: Definition 3.3.7: p. 121 (PDF p. 139). Definition 3.3.9: p. 123 (PDF p. 141). Definition 3.3.2: p. 118 (PDF p. 136)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statements] Definition 3.3.7. Kernel Density Estimator. Let $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ be i.i.d. continuous random variables with common PDF $f$. Let $K : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be an even function$^{32}$ satisfying $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} K(x)dx = 1$, and let $K_h(x) = \frac{1}{h}K(\frac{x}{h})$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$ and $h > 0$. Then a kernel density estimator of $f(x)$ is $\hat f_K(x) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} K_h(x - X_i)$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. The function $K$ is called the kernel and the scaling parameter $h$ is called the bandwidth. [Footnote 32: That is, a function whose graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis, so that $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$, $f(x) = f(-x)$.] Definition 3.3.9. Kernel Plug-In Estimator. The kernel plug-in estimator of $\theta = T(F)$ is $\hat\theta_K = T(\hat F_K)$, where $\hat F_K(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x}\hat f(u)du$. Definition 3.3.2. A statistical functional is a function $T : \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathcal{F}$ is the set of all possible CDFs. [What is refuted] That $T(\hat F_K)$ is defined for every statistical functional $T$ and every kernel $K$ admitted by Definition 3.3.7 (with $\hat f$ read as $\hat f_K$): $\hat F_K$ need not be a CDF. [Counterexample, from the validator] Let $K(t) = 1$ for $|t| \le 1$, $K(t) = -\frac{1}{2}$ for $1 < |t| \le 2$, and $K(t) = 0$ otherwise. $K$ is even, absolutely integrable, and $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} K(t)dt = 2 - 1 = 1$. For $n = 1$, $h = 1$ and any observation $X_1 = a$: $\hat f_K(x) = K(x - a)$, $\hat F_K(a - 1) = \int_{-\infty}^{a-1} K(u - a)du = -\frac{1}{2} < 0$, and $\hat F_K$ is strictly decreasing on $(a - 2, a - 1)$. So $\hat F_K$ is not a CDF. With a fixed functional: for the continuous triangular density supported on $[\frac{5}{4}, \frac{7}{4}]$ and $T(G) = \sqrt{G(0)}$, at $h = 1$ every sample gives $\hat F_K(0) \in [-\frac{3}{8}, -\frac{1}{8}]$, so $T(\hat F_K)$ is undefined with probability one.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random variables and the convention that the unsubscripted $X$ denotes the common distribution (Definition 3.1.1 and p. 92); sample statistic $T_{(n)}$ (Definition 3.2.1); sample mean $\overline{X}$ (Definition 3.2.2); convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); convergence in distribution (Definition 3.2.22); asymptotic normality (Definition 3.2.28); empirical CDF $\hat F$ (Definition 3.3.1); statistical functional and plug-in estimator (Definitions 3.3.2, 3.3.3); and the definitions of Chapters 1 and 2 (expected value, variance, covariance, correlation).
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor: the definition admits signed kernels, for which the integrated estimate is not a CDF; all four kernels illustrated in Figure 3.3.2 are non-negative and no result in the book uses a signed kernel. The validator's numbers are in exact rational arithmetic.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Definition 3.3.9 (Kernel Plug-In Estimator), corrected: a non-negative kernel
canonical_claim.location: p. 123 (PDF p. 141), Definition 3.3.9; Definition 3.3.7, p. 121 (PDF p. 139)
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected statement] Definition 3.3.9. Kernel Plug-In Estimator. The kernel plug-in estimator of $\theta = T(F)$ is $\hat\theta_K = T(\hat F_K)$, where $\hat F_K(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x}\hat f_K(u)du$. For kernel plug-in estimation, assume additionally that $K$ is nonnegative almost everywhere. [Formal content] Let $K : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be an even (measurable) function with $K \ge 0$ almost everywhere and $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} K(x)dx = 1$, let $h > 0$, let $x_1, ..., x_n \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $\hat f_K(x) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{h}K\left(\frac{x - x_i}{h}\right)$ and $\hat F_K(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x}\hat f_K(u)du$. Then $\hat f_K \ge 0$ almost everywhere, $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\hat f_K(u)du = 1$, and $\hat F_K$ is a CDF (nondecreasing, continuous, with limits 0 at $-\infty$ and 1 at $+\infty$); hence $\hat F_K \in \mathcal{F}$ and $T(\hat F_K)$ is defined for every statistical functional $T : \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}$ (Definition 3.3.2).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random variables and the convention that the unsubscripted $X$ denotes the common distribution (Definition 3.1.1 and p. 92); sample statistic $T_{(n)}$ (Definition 3.2.1); sample mean $\overline{X}$ (Definition 3.2.2); convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); convergence in distribution (Definition 3.2.22); asymptotic normality (Definition 3.2.28); empirical CDF $\hat F$ (Definition 3.3.1); statistical functional and plug-in estimator (Definitions 3.3.2, 3.3.3); and the definitions of Chapters 1 and 2 (expected value, variance, covariance, correlation). [Definition 3.3.7, p. 121] Let $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ be i.i.d. continuous random variables with common PDF $f$. Let $K : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be an even function satisfying $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} K(x)dx = 1$, and let $K_h(x) = \frac{1}{h}K(\frac{x}{h})$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$ and $h > 0$. Then a kernel density estimator of $f(x)$ is $\hat f_K(x) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} K_h(x - X_i)$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor. The validator's alternative is to add the condition to Definition 3.3.7 for the whole section; adding it to Definition 3.3.9 keeps signed kernels available for density estimation alone. The integrand is written $\hat f_K$ (the missing subscript is finding P001-C03-N012, separate target).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Definition 3.3.9 (Kernel Plug-In Estimator), last line: the integrand, corrected to the kernel density estimator $\hat f_K$
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed line] where $\hat F_K(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x}\hat f(u)du$. [Corrected line] where $\hat F_K(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x}\hat f_K(u)du$. [Formal content] With $\hat f_K(u) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{h}K\left(\frac{u - X_i}{h}\right)$ as in Definition 3.3.7 and $K$ integrable: $\hat F_K(x) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\int_{-\infty}^{(x - X_i)/h} K(t)dt$ for every $x \in \mathbb{R}$. For the rectangular kernel $K(t) = \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{I}(-1 \le t \le 1)$ of Theorem 3.3.8, $\hat f_K(x) = \frac{\hat F(x + h) - \hat F(x - h)}{2h}$ at every $x$ such that no observation equals $x - h$ (proof sketch, p. 123), where $\hat F$ is the empirical CDF.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random variables and the convention that the unsubscripted $X$ denotes the common distribution (Definition 3.1.1 and p. 92); sample statistic $T_{(n)}$ (Definition 3.2.1); sample mean $\overline{X}$ (Definition 3.2.2); convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); convergence in distribution (Definition 3.2.22); asymptotic normality (Definition 3.2.28); empirical CDF $\hat F$ (Definition 3.3.1); statistical functional and plug-in estimator (Definitions 3.3.2, 3.3.3); and the definitions of Chapters 1 and 2 (expected value, variance, covariance, correlation). [Definition 3.3.7, p. 121 (PDF p. 139)] $K_h(x) = \frac{1}{h}K(\frac{x}{h})$; $\hat f_K(x) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} K_h(x - X_i)$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Example 3.3.4, p. 119 (PDF p. 137)] $\hat f$ denotes the empirical PMF. [Proof sketch of Theorem 3.3.8, p. 123] For any $h > 0$, $K_h(x) = \frac{1}{2h}\mathrm{I}\left(-1 \le \frac{x}{h} \le 1\right) = \frac{\mathrm{I}(-h \le x \le h)}{2h}$. Thus, $\hat f_K(x) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\mathrm{I}(-h \le X_i - x \le h)}{2h} = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{I}(x - h \le X_i \le x + h)}{2h} = \frac{\hat F(x + h) - \hat F(x - h)}{2h}$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor (kind: notation): the subscript $K$ is missing from the integrand; $\hat f$ without subscript was the empirical PMF in Example 3.3.4. This is a correction to a definition; the formal content listed is the change of variables that makes $\hat F_K$ explicit. The last equality of the printed proof sketch, $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i\mathrm{I}(x - h \le X_i \le x + h) = \hat F(x + h) - \hat F(x - h)$, holds when no observation equals $x - h$ (probability one for continuous $X$), which is the proviso stated here.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 3.4.3, the sentence 'Given the usual plug-in regularity conditions (Section 3.3.1), this standard deviation will consistently estimate the standard error', as printed
canonical_claim.location: p. 131 (PDF p. 149), sentence after the four bootstrap steps; Section 3.3.1 and footnote 31, p. 120 (PDF p. 138); Definition 3.2.32, pp. 113–114 (PDF pp. 131–132)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] More specifically, to characterize the uncertainty of our estimator: 1. Take a with replacement sample of size $n$ from our sample. 2. Calculate our would-be estimate using this bootstrap sample. 3. Repeat steps 1 and 2 many times. 4. Using the resulting collection of bootstrap estimates, calculate the standard deviation of the bootstrap distribution of our estimator. Given the usual plug-in regularity conditions (Section 3.3.1), this standard deviation will consistently estimate the standard error. [What is refuted] That regularity of the functional $T$ at $F$ (Section 3.3.1 and footnote 31) implies consistency, in the sense of Definition 3.2.32, of the ideal bootstrap standard deviation: with $\theta = T(F)$, $\hat\theta = T(\hat F)$, $\hat\theta^* = T(\hat F^*)$ for the empirical CDF $\hat F^*$ of $n$ draws with replacement from the sample, and $\mathrm{V}_*$ the variance conditional on the sample, the claim is $n\mathrm{V}_*[\hat\theta^*] \xrightarrow{p} \phi^2$ whenever $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \phi^2)$. The validity of the bootstrap distribution as a weak approximation is not refuted. [Counterexample, from the validator (highest-effort check)] Population: with probability $\frac{1}{2}$, $X$ is uniform on $[-1, 1]$; with probability $\frac{1}{4}$, $X = 2^{1/U^2}$; with probability $\frac{1}{4}$, $X = -2^{1/U^2}$, where $U$ is uniform on $(0, 1)$. Then $\Pr[X \ge x] = \frac{1}{4\sqrt{\log_2 x}}$ for $x \ge 2$, the CDF is $F(x) = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{x}{4}$ for $|x| \le 1$, the median 0 is unique, and with $H_j = 2^{j^2}$: $\Pr[X \ge H_j] = \frac{1}{4j}$. (i) The median: for odd $n = 2k - 1$ let $M_n = X_{(k)}$ be the sample median and $M_n^*$ the median of a bootstrap sample. Then $\sqrt{n}M_n \xrightarrow{d} N(0, 4)$ and, conditionally on the data, $\sqrt{n}(M_n^* - M_n)$ converges weakly in probability to $N(0, 4)$; but for every odd $n \ge 5$, $\Pr\left[n\mathrm{V}_*[M_n^*] > 5\right] \ge \frac{3}{16}$, so $n\mathrm{V}_*[M_n^*]$ does not converge in probability to 4. (ii) A functional that is Hadamard differentiable in every sup-norm direction: $T_0(G) = G(0) - \frac{1}{2}$ if $\frac{1}{4} \le G(0) \le \frac{3}{4}$, and $T_0(G) = \inf\{x : G(x) \ge \frac{1}{2}\}$ otherwise. For $\|G - F\|_\infty < \frac{1}{4}$, $T_0(G) - T_0(F) = G(0) - F(0)$ exactly, so $T_0$ is linear in a sup-norm neighborhood of $F$ and Hadamard differentiable at $F$ with derivative $h \mapsto h(0)$, with no restriction on the direction $h$. Then $\sqrt{n}T_0(\hat F) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \frac{1}{4})$ and the conditional law of $\sqrt{n}(T_0(\hat F^*) - T_0(\hat F))$ converges weakly in probability to $N(0, \frac{1}{4})$, but on the event $E_n$ used for the median (an observation $a \ge H_n$ and an observation $b \in [-1, 1]$) the resample repeating $a$ gives $T_0 = a$ and the resample repeating $b$ gives $T_0 = b$, so again $\Pr\left[n\mathrm{V}_*[T_0(\hat F^*)] > 5\right] \ge \frac{3}{16}$ for every odd $n \ge 5$, and $n\mathrm{V}_*[T_0(\hat F^*)]$ does not converge in probability to $\frac{1}{4}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random variables and the convention that the unsubscripted $X$ denotes the common distribution (Definition 3.1.1 and p. 92); sample statistic $T_{(n)}$ (Definition 3.2.1); sample mean $\overline{X}$ (Definition 3.2.2); convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); convergence in distribution (Definition 3.2.22); asymptotic normality (Definition 3.2.28); empirical CDF $\hat F$ (Definition 3.3.1); statistical functional and plug-in estimator (Definitions 3.3.2, 3.3.3); and the definitions of Chapters 1 and 2 (expected value, variance, covariance, correlation). [Definition 3.2.32, pp. 113–114, as corrected under P001-C03-N007] For an estimator $\hat\theta$ such that $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} T$, a standard error estimator $\sqrt{\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\hat\theta]}$ is consistent if $\sqrt{n}\sqrt{\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\hat\theta]} \xrightarrow{p} \sqrt{\mathrm{V}[T]}$. [Footnote 31, p. 120] $T$ is well behaved if it is Hadamard differentiable at $F$ with respect to the Kolmogorov distance. [Notation of the validator] $\mathrm{E}_*$, $\mathrm{V}_*$: expectation and variance over the $n$-out-of-$n$ resampling, conditional on the observations; the 'ideal' bootstrap standard deviation is $\sqrt{\mathrm{V}_*[\hat\theta^*]}$ (infinitely many repetitions of steps 1–2).
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: [Exact, for each $n$; from the validator's derivation, Section 3] Let $E_n$ be the event that some observation is $\ge H_n$ and some observation lies in $[-1, 1]$. Then $\Pr[E_n] = 1 - (1 - \frac{1}{4n})^n - 2^{-n} + (\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{4n})^n$ and, for $n \ge 5$, $\Pr[E_n] \ge \frac{7}{32} + \frac{1}{32n} - 2^{-n} \ge \frac{3}{16}$. On $E_n$, a bootstrap sample that repeats one index $n$ times has probability $n^{-n}$, so with $a \ge H_n$ and $b \in [-1, 1]$ two observations, $\mathrm{V}_*[M_n^*] = \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{E}_*[(Y - Y')^2] \ge n^{-2n}(H_n - 1)^2 \ge 2^{-2n(n-1)}2^{2n^2-2} = 2^{2n-2}$ (using $n \le 2^{n-1}$ and $H_n - 1 \ge 2^{n^2-1}$), where $Y, Y'$ are independent conditional copies of $M_n^*$. Hence $n\mathrm{V}_*[M_n^*] \ge n2^{2n-2} > 5$ on $E_n$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor. The first validation confirmed the finding; an intermediate reading treated it as a clarity issue; the highest-effort check (runs/P001/validate/P001-C03-N016/doubt/doubt.json) restored the confirmation: the natural referent of the 'usual plug-in regularity conditions' is the functional $T$, and its regularity does not give convergence of bootstrap second moments. The counterexample needs heavy tails; for the book's finite-variance means the bootstrap standard deviation is consistent. The finite-sample median here has infinite variance; Definition 3.2.32 uses the variance of the root-$n$ limit, which is 4.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 3.4.3, consistency of the bootstrap standard deviation for the standard error, corrected: the added moment condition
canonical_claim.location: p. 131 (PDF p. 149), sentence after the four bootstrap steps; Definition 3.2.32, pp. 113–114 (PDF pp. 131–132)
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected statement] Given the usual plug-in regularity conditions (Section 3.3.1) and a moment condition on the bootstrap distribution, this standard deviation will consistently estimate the standard error. [In full] Let $\hat\theta$ be an estimator with $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \phi^2)$, $0 < \phi < \infty$, let $\hat\theta^*$ be the estimate computed from an $n$-out-of-$n$ bootstrap sample, and let $Z_n^* = \sqrt{n}(\hat\theta^* - \hat\theta)$, with $\mathrm{E}_*$ and $\mathrm{V}_*$ the conditional expectation and variance given the observations (finite for each sample). Suppose (W) the conditional law of $Z_n^*$ converges weakly in probability to $N(0, \phi^2)$, and (M) for every $\epsilon > 0$, $\lim_{K \to \infty}\limsup_{n \to \infty}\Pr\left\{\mathrm{E}_*\left[(Z_n^*)^2\mathbb{1}\{|Z_n^*| > K\}\right] > \epsilon\right\} = 0$. Then $n\mathrm{V}_*[\hat\theta^*] \xrightarrow{p} \phi^2$ and $\sqrt{n}\sqrt{\mathrm{V}_*[\hat\theta^*]} \xrightarrow{p} \phi$; that is, the ideal bootstrap standard deviation is a consistent standard error estimator in the sense of Definition 3.2.32. Conversely, given (W), $n\mathrm{V}_*[\hat\theta^*] \xrightarrow{p} \phi^2$ implies (M). [Cases, from the validator] For the sample mean of i.i.d. variables with finite variance $\mathrm{V}[X] > 0$, $n\mathrm{V}_*[\overline{X}^*] = \overline{X^2} - \overline{X}^2$ exactly, which converges in probability to $\mathrm{V}[X]$ (Theorem 3.2.19), so the conclusion holds with no added condition. For the median with a positive continuous density near a unique median, $\mathrm{E}|X|^\eta < \infty$ for some $\eta > 0$ is a sufficient primitive condition.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random variables and the convention that the unsubscripted $X$ denotes the common distribution (Definition 3.1.1 and p. 92); sample statistic $T_{(n)}$ (Definition 3.2.1); sample mean $\overline{X}$ (Definition 3.2.2); convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); convergence in distribution (Definition 3.2.22); asymptotic normality (Definition 3.2.28); empirical CDF $\hat F$ (Definition 3.3.1); statistical functional and plug-in estimator (Definitions 3.3.2, 3.3.3); and the definitions of Chapters 1 and 2 (expected value, variance, covariance, correlation). [Bootstrap procedure, p. 131] 1. Take a with replacement sample of size $n$ from our sample. 2. Calculate our would-be estimate using this bootstrap sample. 3. Repeat steps 1 and 2 many times. 4. Using the resulting collection of bootstrap estimates, calculate the standard deviation of the bootstrap distribution of our estimator. [Definition 3.2.32, as corrected] a standard error estimator $\sqrt{\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\hat\theta]}$ is consistent if $\sqrt{n}\sqrt{\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\hat\theta]} \xrightarrow{p} \sqrt{\mathrm{V}[T]}$, where $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} T$. [Weak convergence in probability] for every bounded continuous $g$, $\mathrm{E}_*[g(Z_n^*)] \xrightarrow{p} \mathrm{E}[g(Z)]$ with $Z \sim N(0, \phi^2)$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: [Truncation steps, exact for each $n$ and $K > 0$; validator's derivation, Section 2] with $q_K(z) = \min(z^2, K^2)$ and $a_K(z) = \max(-K, \min(z, K))$: $0 \le \mathrm{E}_*[(Z_n^*)^2] - \mathrm{E}_*[q_K(Z_n^*)] \le \mathrm{E}_*[(Z_n^*)^2\mathbb{1}\{|Z_n^*| > K\}]$ and $|\mathrm{E}_*[Z_n^*] - \mathrm{E}_*[a_K(Z_n^*)]| \le K^{-1}\mathrm{E}_*[(Z_n^*)^2\mathbb{1}\{|Z_n^*| > K\}]$; $\mathrm{V}_*[Z_n^*] = \mathrm{E}_*[(Z_n^*)^2] - (\mathrm{E}_*[Z_n^*])^2 = n\mathrm{V}_*[\hat\theta^*]$. For the sample mean: $\mathrm{E}_*[\overline{X}^*] = \overline{X}$ and $\mathrm{V}_*[\overline{X}^*] = \frac{1}{n}(\overline{X^2} - \overline{X}^2)$ for every sample.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor: the missing condition is mild and holds automatically for the finite-variance means of the book's examples and simulations. A finite number of bootstrap repetitions adds a separate Monte Carlo requirement ($n|\hat V_{MC} - \mathrm{V}_*| \xrightarrow{p} 0$), which the book does not address. Headline claim P001-ch03-H8 (the bootstrap 'consistently estimates the standard error under the usual plug-in regularity conditions') holds with this added condition.
